name: agent-mq

hlido_opinion.headline: An early (v0.2), MCP-native message queue that lets AI coding assistants talk to each other across tools — a clean idea with a thin, unproven surface.
hlido_opinion.body: agent-mq is a small, honestly-presented message queue aimed at cross-tool agent communication: any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can send and receive messages so agents running in different tools can coordinate. The premise is good and increasingly relevant — as people run several coding assistants at once, a shared, tool-agnostic message bus is a real gap. The surface shows the right primitives: seven MCP tools, a one-npx install, UUID-based namespace isolation (same token = same namespace, different tokens can't see each other), and self-hosting via Docker or a hosted server. What holds it back is maturity and evidence: it is version 0.2.0, the on-page counters are tiny (8 users, 25 agents, 24 messages), and the landing page is essentially an install pitch — there is no visible detail on delivery guarantees, ordering, persistence, or security beyond the namespace-isolation line. For an early adopter comfortable with a young MIT project this is worth a look; for anything load-bearing it is too early to trust from the public surface.

tier_rationale: FADING (58) reflects a genuinely useful idea (cross-tool, MCP-native agent messaging) at a very early stage: v0.2.0, single-digit users, and a landing page that is mostly an install call-to-action with little evidence of delivery semantics, persistence or security. Not lower because the core primitives (7 MCP tools, UUID namespace isolation, self-hostable, MIT) are real and sensibly chosen. Not STEADY because nothing about reliability, scale or adoption is demonstrated, and the surface is too thin to verify the claims that would make it dependable.
what_it_does_well: MCP-native cross-tool messaging: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or anything that can run a bash command
UUID-based namespace isolation — same token shares a namespace, different tokens are mutually invisible
Self-hostable (Docker) as well as a hosted option; MIT-licensed
Low-friction adoption: seven MCP tools installed via a single npx command
what_it_fails_at: Very early: v0.2.0 with tiny on-page usage counters (8 users / 25 agents / 24 messages)
No visible detail on delivery guarantees, message ordering, persistence, durability or throughput
Security posture beyond token-based namespace isolation is not described on the surface
Landing page is essentially an install pitch — little documentation or evidence of production use is exposed
best_for: Early adopters wiring up experiments where several AI coding assistants need to pass messages
Developers who want a self-hostable, MIT-licensed agent message bus and are comfortable with a v0.x tool
Prototyping multi-agent, multi-tool coordination without building queue infrastructure
not_recommended_for: Any load-bearing or production workload needing delivery/ordering/durability guarantees
Teams with strict security/compliance requirements (isolation model is minimal on the surface)
Users who need proven scale, support or a stable API — this is pre-1.0
red_flags: v0.2.0 with single-digit usage — treat as experimental; do not build anything you cannot afford to lose on it yet.
Delivery semantics, persistence and security are not evidenced on the public surface, so reliability is unknown.
